dx: Denys-Drash syndrome with Wilms tumor and diffuse mesangial sclerosis
case: An 18-month-old child is brought to the physician because of swelling of the eyelids and legs for 3 weeks and an abdominal mass the parents felt while bathing the child. The child was born with ambiguous genitalia, and karyotype is 46,XY. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg (above the 95th percentile for age). There is pitting edema of both legs and a firm, smooth left flank mass. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL (3.5 to 5.0), serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL (0.2 to 0.4), and the urine protein to creatinine ratio is 6.5 mg/mg (below 0.2). Biopsy of the right kidney shows diffuse mesangial sclerosis. The left kidney mass is resected and shows Wilms tumor. The diagnosis is Denys-Drash syndrome.

questions.stem: Genetic testing is performed. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Missense mutation in a WT1 zinc finger
Loss of imprinting at 11p15 with IGF2 overexpression
Germline inactivation of VHL on chromosome 3p
approach: Pick out the triad: early nephrotic syndrome with diffuse mesangial sclerosis, 46,XY disorder of sex development, and Wilms tumor.
That triad is Denys-Drash syndrome, a disorder of WT1 on 11p13.
Recall that Denys-Drash comes from a point mutation in WT1, while WAGR comes from a larger deletion that also removes PAX6.
questions.why: Denys-Drash syndrome is caused by a heterozygous germline point mutation in WT1, usually a missense change in the zinc finger region that binds DNA. The mutant protein interferes with the normal copy (a dominant-negative effect), so kidney and gonad development are badly disturbed. That explains the severe early nephropathy and the 46,XY child with ambiguous genitalia. The second hit in WT1 in a kidney cell then gives rise to Wilms tumor.
whyNot: A contiguous 11p13 deletion that removes both WT1 and PAX6 causes WAGR syndrome. Those children have aniridia and intellectual disability, and this child has neither.
Correct.

Loss of imprinting at 11p15 with IGF2 overexpression causes Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, with macroglossia, hemihypertrophy, and organomegaly. It does not cause gonadal dysgenesis or diffuse mesangial sclerosis.
Germline VHL loss causes von Hippel-Lindau disease, with clear cell renal cell carcinoma in adults and hemangioblastomas. It is not linked to Wilms tumor or disorders of sex development.

questions.stem: Before resection, the differential diagnosis included neuroblastoma. Which of the following findings would have most supported Wilms tumor?
options: Encasement of the aorta and its branches
Stippled calcification in a suprarenal mass
Mass arising within the renal parenchyma
approach: Wilms tumor and neuroblastoma are the two common abdominal malignancies of early childhood.
Wilms tumor grows inside the kidney and pushes the collecting system aside. Neuroblastoma usually starts in the adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain.
Choose the finding that places the mass within the kidney itself.
questions.why: Wilms tumor arises from the renal parenchyma (from persistent metanephric blastema), so imaging shows a mass inside the kidney with a rim of renal tissue around it. It usually presents at 2 to 5 years of age, earlier in syndromes like Denys-Drash, as a large, smooth, unilateral flank mass that often does not cross the midline, sometimes with hematuria or hypertension. Neuroblastoma is a neural crest tumor outside the kidney that tends to calcify, wrap around vessels, and secrete catecholamines.
whyNot: Wrapping around the aorta and its branches is typical of neuroblastoma, which grows along the sympathetic chain. Wilms tumor tends to displace vessels instead.
Raised urinary vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid come from catecholamine production by neuroblastoma. Wilms tumor does not make catecholamines.
Stippled calcification in an adrenal (suprarenal) mass points to neuroblastoma. Calcification is uncommon in Wilms tumor.
Correct.

questions.stem: WT1 is expressed in the metanephric mesenchyme and is required for that tissue to survive and respond to induction. It is not expressed in the ureteric bud. When WT1 function is lost early in development, collecting ducts also fail to form. Which of the following best explains the loss of collecting ducts?
options: Lost mesenchymal signals for bud branching
Failed bud induction of nephron formation
Absent WT1 activity in ureteric bud cells
Mesenchymal origin of collecting duct cells
approach: Recall which tissue makes which part: the ureteric bud forms collecting ducts, calyces, pelvis, and ureter, and the metanephric mesenchyme forms the nephron from Bowman capsule to the distal convoluted tubule.
Induction runs both ways. The mesenchyme signals the bud to grow and branch (GDNF acting on RET), and the bud signals the mesenchyme to form nephrons.
If the mesenchyme dies, the bud loses the signal it needs to branch, so no collecting system forms either.
questions.why: Kidney formation depends on reciprocal induction. The metanephric mesenchyme secretes GDNF, which binds the RET receptor on the ureteric bud and drives the bud to grow and branch into collecting ducts. The branching bud in turn induces the mesenchyme to form nephrons. WT1 keeps the mesenchyme alive and competent, so without it the bud receives no branching signal, and both halves of the kidney fail. A complete failure of this induction produces renal agenesis.
whyNot: Correct.
The signal from the bud to the mesenchyme explains why nephrons form. Losing it would explain absent nephrons, but it does not explain why the bud itself fails to make collecting ducts.
The stem states WT1 is not expressed in the ureteric bud, so the bud cells do not depend on their own WT1. Their failure comes from losing signals from the mesenchyme.

Collecting ducts come from the ureteric bud, which is an outgrowth of the mesonephric duct. Only the nephron, from Bowman capsule to the distal convoluted tubule, comes from the metanephric mesenchyme.

topics: Ureteric bud vs metanephric mesenchyme derivatives

questions.stem: The intermediate mesoderm gives rise to three kidney systems in sequence. The permanent kidney begins when an outgrowth from the duct of an earlier kidney grows into the metanephric blastema. From which of the following structures does this outgrowth arise?
approach: Put the three kidneys in order: pronephros (rudimentary, gone by the end of week 4), mesonephros (a temporary interim kidney), and metanephros (the permanent kidney, from week 5).
The outgrowth that invades the metanephric blastema is the ureteric bud.
The ureteric bud sprouts from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct near its entry into the cloaca.
questions.why: The pronephros is a rudimentary structure that regresses during week 4. The mesonephros works briefly as an interim kidney, and its duct (the mesonephric or Wolffian duct) persists. In the fifth week the ureteric bud grows out of the mesonephric duct and penetrates the metanephric blastema, starting the metanephros. In males the rest of the mesonephric duct later forms the epididymis, ductus deferens, and seminal vesicles.
whyNot: The paramesonephric (Mullerian) duct forms the uterine tubes, uterus, and upper vagina. It does not give rise to the ureteric bud.
The urogenital sinus forms most of the bladder and the urethra. The ureters open into it, but they do not grow out of it.
Correct.
The pronephric tubules are rudimentary and regress by the end of week 4. They do not contribute to the permanent kidney.

dx: Bladder adenocarcinoma arising in a urachal remnant
case: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of blood in his urine for 2 months and passage of thick mucus at the end of urination. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg. A firm, nontender midline mass is palpable just above the pubic symphysis. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood and mucus strands. Colonoscopy is normal. CT shows a partly calcified mass at the bladder dome that extends along the anterior abdominal wall toward the umbilicus. Cystoscopic biopsy shows mucin-producing adenocarcinoma with enteric-type glands. The urothelium away from the dome is normal. The diagnosis is adenocarcinoma of the bladder arising in a urachal remnant.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions predisposes to bladder cancer of the same histologic type as this patient's tumor?
approach: Name the histologic type: glandular, mucin-producing tumor, so adenocarcinoma.
Recall that bladder adenocarcinoma is linked to urachal remnants and bladder exstrophy, squamous cell carcinoma to chronic irritation, and urothelial carcinoma to chemical carcinogens.
Choose the condition tied to adenocarcinoma.
questions.why: Primary adenocarcinoma of the bladder is uncommon. It arises in two classic settings: urachal remnants at the dome, as in this patient, and bladder exstrophy. In exstrophy the exposed bladder mucosa is chronically inflamed and undergoes glandular (intestinal-type) metaplasia, which can progress to adenocarcinoma. Urachal tumors tend to sit at the dome, extend toward the umbilicus, and make mucin, which can appear in the urine.
whyNot: Schistosoma haematobium eggs lodge in the bladder wall and cause chronic inflammation with squamous metaplasia, so the linked cancer is squamous cell carcinoma.
Cyclophosphamide is broken down to acrolein, which causes hemorrhagic cystitis and raises the risk of urothelial carcinoma.
A long-term indwelling catheter or bladder stones cause chronic irritation and squamous metaplasia, so they predispose to squamous cell carcinoma.
Correct.

topics: Bladder cancer histologic types and risk factors

questions.stem: The urachus connects the apex of the developing bladder to the umbilicus. Between the fourth and seventh weeks, the urorectal septum divides the cloaca. Which of the following structures formed by this partition gives rise to most of the bladder?
approach: The urorectal septum splits the cloaca into an anterior part and a posterior part.
The posterior part is the anorectal canal. The anterior part is the urogenital sinus.
The upper (vesical) part of the urogenital sinus becomes the bladder, which stays joined to the allantois at its apex through the urachus.
questions.why: The cloaca is the endoderm-lined end of the hindgut. The urorectal septum grows down and divides it into the anorectal canal behind and the urogenital sinus in front. The upper part of the urogenital sinus forms most of the bladder, and the lower parts form the urethra. The allantois, attached at the bladder apex, narrows into the urachus and normally becomes a fibrous cord, the median umbilical ligament. If the urachus stays open, urine drains from the umbilicus, and if part of it persists, a cyst or a tumor like this one can arise.
whyNot: Correct.
The anorectal canal is the posterior product of the partition and forms the rectum and upper anal canal.
The allantois is the outpouching that narrows into the urachus. It is the source of the remnant where this tumor arose, and it does not form the bladder wall itself.
The mesonephric ducts are absorbed into the back wall of the bladder and help form the trigone. They are not a product of cloacal partition and do not form most of the bladder.

questions.stem: Before biopsy, urothelial carcinoma was thought most likely because he worked for 20 years in a plant that made aniline dyes containing 2-naphthylamine and benzidine. Which of the following best explains how this exposure injures the urothelium?
options: Direct alkylation of DNA by the inhaled parent amine
Squamous metaplasia from chronic mucosal irritation
Urinary release of hepatically activated metabolites
Acrolein formation from amine breakdown in urine
approach: Aromatic amines are procarcinogens. They need metabolic activation before they can damage DNA.
The liver N-hydroxylates them and conjugates them, and the conjugates are excreted in urine.
In the bladder the conjugates break down and release reactive metabolites that form DNA adducts in the urothelium, which is bathed in stored urine.
questions.why: Aromatic amines such as 2-naphthylamine and benzidine are hydroxylated by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes and then conjugated for excretion. In urine, the conjugates are hydrolyzed and release reactive N-hydroxy metabolites that bind DNA in urothelial cells. Because urine sits in the bladder, the whole urothelial surface is exposed, which is why urothelial carcinoma linked to these chemicals tends to be multifocal and recur. Slow acetylators clear these amines less well and carry a higher risk.
whyNot: The parent amines are inert until they are metabolized, and the damage happens where the activated metabolites are concentrated, in the urine.
Squamous metaplasia from chronic irritation (stones, catheters, schistosomiasis) leads to squamous cell carcinoma. Aromatic amines act as chemical carcinogens on the urothelium.
Correct.
Acrolein is the urotoxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide. It is not formed from aromatic amines.

questions.stem: Ten years ago, he sustained a pelvic ring fracture in a fall, and a bone fragment tore the anterolateral wall of his bladder near the bladder neck. The peritoneum was intact. Into which of the following spaces did urine most likely leak?
approach: The bladder is extraperitoneal. Only its superior surface (the dome) is covered by peritoneum.
A pelvic fracture tears the lower anterior or lateral wall, below the peritoneal covering.
Urine from that tear spreads in the extraperitoneal fat in front of and around the bladder, the retropubic space.
questions.why: The kidneys and ureters are retroperitoneal, and the bladder sits below the peritoneum in the pelvis with only its dome covered by peritoneum. Pelvic fractures injure the bladder near the neck or the anterolateral wall, so urine escapes into the extraperitoneal retropubic (prevesical) space and can track into the thigh, scrotum, or abdominal wall. A blow to a full bladder bursts the dome instead, and urine then enters the peritoneal cavity.
whyNot: The rectovesical pouch is part of the peritoneal cavity. Urine would collect there after an intraperitoneal dome rupture.
Correct.
The paracolic gutters are peritoneal spaces beside the colon. Urine reaches them only after intraperitoneal rupture of the dome.
The perirenal space surrounds the kidney within the renal fascia. A kidney or upper ureter injury would leak urine there.

dx: Proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis with Fanconi syndrome from Wilson disease
case: A 19-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a hand tremor, worsening handwriting, and fatigue for 3 months. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Slit-lamp examination shows Kayser-Fleischer rings. Serum studies show sodium 139 mEq/L (136 to 145), potassium 3.0 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), chloride 114 mEq/L (98 to 106), bicarbonate 17 mEq/L (22 to 28), glucose 86 mg/dL (70 to 99), phosphate 1.9 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), ALT 88 U/L (7 to 35), and ceruloplasmin 9 mg/dL (20 to 35). Urinalysis shows pH 5.4, 2+ glucose, and trace protein. Urine amino acids are increased. The diagnosis is proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis as part of Fanconi syndrome caused by Wilson disease.

questions.stem: If her tubular defect persists untreated, which of the following complications is most likely?
approach: Fanconi syndrome means the proximal tubule fails to reabsorb glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, and urate.
Phosphate wasting lowers serum phosphate, and chronic acidosis pulls buffer from bone.
Low phosphate in an adult whose growth plates have closed leads to poor mineralization of bone, which is osteomalacia.
questions.why: In Fanconi syndrome the proximal tubule loses its ability to reclaim filtered phosphate, so serum phosphate stays low. The injured proximal tubule may also make less calcitriol, and chronic metabolic acidosis releases buffer from bone. Without enough phosphate, newly formed osteoid cannot mineralize, causing rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, with bone pain and fractures. Wilson disease, cystinosis, and multiple myeloma are classic causes.
whyNot: Correct.
Metastatic calcification needs a high calcium-phosphate product, as in hyperphosphatemia of chronic kidney disease. Her phosphate is low.

Fanconi syndrome wastes urate, so serum uric acid is low. Stones are uncommon in Fanconi syndrome, and its classic long-term complication is bone disease from phosphate wasting. Uric acid stones are typical of gout and tumor lysis, where serum urate is high.
Proximal RTA causes hypokalemia from increased distal sodium delivery and aldosterone effect. Hyperkalemia goes with type 4 RTA.

questions.stem: Sodium bicarbonate is infused to localize her acidification defect. As her serum bicarbonate rises from 17 to 23 mEq/L, her urine pH rises from 5.4 to 7.6, and the fractional excretion of bicarbonate rises to 18 percent (normally below 5 percent at a normal serum bicarbonate). Which of the following best explains these findings?
options: Impaired H+ secretion by alpha-intercalated cells
Reduced aldosterone action in the collecting duct
Back-leak of secreted H+ across distal epithelium
approach: At her low serum bicarbonate, the filtered load is small enough that her damaged proximal tubule can reclaim it, so the urine is acidic (pH 5.4).
Raising serum bicarbonate above her lowered threshold floods the tubule, and large amounts spill into the urine.
A high fractional excretion of bicarbonate after loading points to a proximal defect.
questions.why: In type 2 RTA the proximal tubule has a lower threshold for bicarbonate reabsorption. Serum bicarbonate falls until the filtered load matches what the tubule can reclaim, and then the distal nephron, which works normally, acidifies the urine below pH 5.5. When bicarbonate is given, the filtered load exceeds the proximal threshold, bicarbonate pours into the urine, and the fractional excretion rises above about 15 percent. Distal (type 1) RTA behaves differently: urine pH stays above 5.5 at every serum bicarbonate.
whyNot: Impaired H+ secretion by alpha-intercalated cells is type 1 (distal) RTA. Those patients cannot lower urine pH below 5.5 even when acidemic, and her baseline urine pH was 5.4.
Reduced aldosterone action causes type 4 RTA with hyperkalemia and acidic urine. She is hypokalemic.
Correct.
H+ back-leak across the distal epithelium (as with amphotericin B) is a form of distal RTA. It keeps urine pH above 5.5 during acidemia.

questions.stem: Copper accumulates in her proximal tubule cells and injures their mitochondria. Which of the following best explains how this injury causes glucose to appear in her urine?
options: Filtered glucose load above the transport maximum
Loss of insulin-dependent tubular glucose uptake
Loss of the Na+ gradient driving apical uptake
approach: Her plasma glucose is normal, so the filtered load is normal and below the usual renal threshold of about 200 mg/dL.
Proximal glucose uptake uses SGLT2, a sodium-glucose cotransporter driven by the low sodium concentration inside the cell.
That low intracellular sodium is kept up by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, which needs ATP from mitochondria. Without ATP, the drive for glucose uptake fails.
questions.why: Glucose is freely filtered and normally almost all of it is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by SGLT2 (with SGLT1 further along). This is secondary active transport: glucose rides into the cell with sodium down the sodium gradient, which the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase creates by using ATP. Proximal cells are packed with mitochondria to meet this demand. When copper damages the mitochondria, ATP falls, the sodium gradient collapses, and glucose, amino acids, and phosphate all spill into the urine even though plasma glucose is normal.
whyNot: A filtered load above the transport maximum causes glucosuria in poorly controlled diabetes, when plasma glucose exceeds about 200 mg/dL. Her plasma glucose is 86 mg/dL.
Glucose is a small molecule that is already freely filtered, so a change in glomerular permeability would not raise the amount reaching the tubule.
Proximal tubule glucose uptake does not depend on insulin. It is driven by the sodium gradient.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the normal proximal tubule reclaims most filtered bicarbonate, the process that fails in this patient?
options: Paracellular diffusion driven by lumen-positive voltage
Na+/H+ exchange with luminal carbonic anhydrase
Apical uptake of intact HCO3- through anion channels
approach: Recall that the proximal tubule reclaims about 80 to 90 percent of filtered bicarbonate, along with about two thirds of filtered sodium and water.
The apical Na+/H+ exchanger secretes H+, which combines with filtered HCO3- to form carbonic acid.
Luminal carbonic anhydrase splits it into CO2 and water, which enter the cell, where bicarbonate is regenerated and leaves across the basolateral membrane.
questions.why: Filtered bicarbonate is not taken up directly. The apical Na+/H+ exchanger, powered by the sodium gradient, secretes H+ into the lumen. The H+ joins filtered HCO3-, and carbonic anhydrase on the brush border converts the carbonic acid to CO2 and water. CO2 diffuses into the cell, intracellular carbonic anhydrase rebuilds HCO3-, and it exits to the blood with sodium. Acetazolamide blocks carbonic anhydrase and produces a bicarbonate leak much like proximal RTA.
whyNot: Paracellular transport driven by a lumen-positive voltage reabsorbs Mg2+ and Ca2+ in the thick ascending limb. It is not how bicarbonate is reclaimed.
Correct.
H+-ATPase in alpha-intercalated cells of the collecting duct makes new bicarbonate and acidifies urine. That is the distal step that fails in type 1 RTA.
Bicarbonate is not taken up across the apical membrane as an intact ion. It is converted to CO2 in the lumen first.

dx: Contrast-induced acute tubular necrosis in a man with diabetes after coronary angiography
case: A 64-year-old man with an 18-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus undergoes coronary angiography for unstable angina and receives 250 mL of iodinated contrast. Before the procedure, his serum creatinine was 1.9 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3) and his urine albumin to creatinine ratio was 420 mg/g (below 30). Two days later his urine output falls to 350 mL/day. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 3.6 mg/dL. Urine sediment shows muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells. The fractional excretion of sodium is 2.8 percent (below 1 percent in prerenal states). The diagnosis is contrast-induced acute tubular necrosis superimposed on diabetic nephropathy.

questions.stem: Iodinated contrast causes intense vasoconstriction in the renal medulla and is directly toxic to tubular cells. Which of the following tubule segments is most likely to show the most severe injury?
options: Inner medullary thin descending limb of Henle
approach: Ischemic and toxic tubular injury hits segments that combine heavy active transport with a poor oxygen supply.
The outer medulla gets little blood flow from the vasa recta, and the straight proximal tubule (S3) and medullary thick ascending limb there use a lot of ATP.
Medullary vasoconstriction from contrast makes this region the most vulnerable.
questions.why: Acute tubular necrosis concentrates in the straight segment of the proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb, both in the outer medulla. These cells run energy-hungry pumps, and the outer medulla normally has low oxygen tension because vasa recta flow is slow. Contrast adds medullary vasoconstriction and direct toxicity. The injured cells die and slough, block the lumen, and appear in the urine as muddy brown granular casts.
whyNot: The thin descending limb has a thin squamous lining with little active transport, so it needs little oxygen and is relatively spared.
The cortical collecting duct sits in well-perfused cortex and has a lower transport workload, so it is less vulnerable.
Correct.
The distal convoluted tubule lies in the well-oxygenated cortex and is less affected than the outer medullary segments.

questions.stem: On day 5, his urine output is still 300 mL/day, and he has gained 3 kg. Which of the following sets of serum findings is most likely?
options: Low K+, low HCO3-, low phosphate
High K+, low HCO3-, high phosphate
High K+, high HCO3-, low phosphate
Low K+, high HCO3-, high phosphate
approach: Persistent oliguria with weight gain means he is in the maintenance phase of acute tubular necrosis.
With a low GFR and damaged tubules, he cannot excrete potassium, acid, or phosphate.
Expect hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis with a low bicarbonate, and hyperphosphatemia.
questions.why: Acute tubular necrosis passes through three phases. In the initiation phase, injury occurs and urine output starts to fall. In the maintenance phase, which lasts about 1 to 2 weeks, GFR stays low, so the kidney retains potassium, H+, phosphate, and water, causing hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperphosphatemia, and volume overload. In the recovery phase, GFR returns before the tubules regain full function, so urine output rises and potassium and sodium are lost.
whyNot: Low potassium and low phosphate fit renal wasting, as in the recovery phase or Fanconi syndrome. The oliguric phase retains these.
Correct.
A high bicarbonate means metabolic alkalosis, which does not occur when the kidney cannot excrete acid. Phosphate also rises in oliguric kidney failure.
Low potassium with a high bicarbonate fits vomiting or diuretic use. An oliguric kidney retains potassium and acid.

questions.stem: Early in the course of his diabetes, when his serum creatinine was normal, his measured GFR was 160 mL/min/1.73 m2 (about 90 to 125). Which of the following best explains this hyperfiltration?
options: Glycation-induced loss of basement membrane charge
Higher oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries
Proximal Na+-glucose uptake lowering distal NaCl
approach: In hyperglycemia, more glucose is filtered, and the proximal tubule reabsorbs it along with sodium through SGLT2.
Extra proximal sodium reabsorption leaves less NaCl reaching the macula densa.
Tubuloglomerular feedback reads this as low flow and dilates the afferent arteriole, raising glomerular pressure and GFR.
questions.why: Hyperfiltration is the first stage of diabetic nephropathy. The large filtered glucose load increases sodium-glucose cotransport in the proximal tubule, so less NaCl reaches the macula densa. Tubuloglomerular feedback then dilates the afferent arteriole, and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, raising glomerular capillary pressure and GFR. Over years this pressure, together with nonenzymatic glycation and hyaline arteriolosclerosis, thickens the basement membrane, expands the mesangium, and leads from microalbuminuria to overt proteinuria.
whyNot: Glycation changes the basement membrane and raises its leakiness to albumin. It does not increase the volume of filtrate.
Mesangial expansion crowds the capillary loops and reduces the filtration surface. It comes later and lowers GFR.
Higher oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries opposes filtration and would lower GFR.
Correct.

questions.stem: Ten days later, he develops pneumonia, and gentamicin is considered. Which of the following best explains how this drug would add to his tubular injury?
options: Megalin-mediated uptake into proximal tubule cells
Afferent arteriolar constriction from prostaglandin loss
Crystal precipitation within collecting duct lumens
Hapten-driven T-cell infiltration of the interstitium
approach: Aminoglycosides are a classic nephrotoxic cause of acute tubular necrosis.
They are positively charged and freely filtered, and they bind megalin on the proximal tubule brush border.
After endocytosis they build up in lysosomes and kill the cell.
questions.why: Gentamicin is filtered and then taken up by proximal tubule cells through the megalin-cubilin endocytic receptor on the brush border. It collects in lysosomes, disrupts phospholipid handling, and injures mitochondria, leading to necrosis of proximal tubule cells. Damage typically appears after about 5 to 7 days of therapy and is often nonoliguric. Other nephrotoxic causes of tubular necrosis include iodinated contrast, cisplatin, myoglobin, hemoglobin, and ethylene glycol.
whyNot: Correct.
Loss of vasodilator prostaglandins with afferent constriction is how NSAIDs lower GFR, especially in volume-depleted patients. Gentamicin does not act this way.
Crystal precipitation in tubules is the mechanism of acyclovir, methotrexate, and ethylene glycol (calcium oxalate) injury.
A hapten-driven T-cell infiltrate describes drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis, as from penicillins or proton pump inhibitors.

dx: NSAID-induced acute interstitial nephritis in an older woman with osteoarthritis
case: A 71-year-old woman with osteoarthritis of both knees comes to the physician because of fatigue, poor appetite, and ankle swelling for 1 week. Five weeks ago, she began taking naproxen 500 mg twice daily for knee pain. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg. A faint maculopapular rash is present on the trunk. Serum creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), up from 0.9 mg/dL 3 months ago. Leukocyte count is 8600/mm3 with 9 percent eosinophils (1 to 4). Urinalysis shows trace protein and 15 to 20 leukocytes per high-power field with no bacteria, and urine culture is negative. Renal biopsy shows interstitial edema with lymphocytes and eosinophils invading the tubules and normal glomeruli. The diagnosis is NSAID-induced acute interstitial nephritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following cytokines, released by activated helper T cells, most directly accounts for the eosinophils in her blood and renal interstitium?
approach: Drug-induced interstitial nephritis is a hypersensitivity reaction that appears days to weeks after a drug is started.
The drug acts as an antigen that activates helper T cells, and eosinophils in blood and tissue show a Th2 component.
The Th2 cytokine that drives eosinophil production and activation is IL-5.
questions.why: In drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis, the drug or a drug-protein complex is presented to helper T cells, which infiltrate the interstitium and attack tubules. Th2 cells release IL-5, which drives eosinophil production in the marrow and recruits and activates eosinophils, giving the blood and tissue eosinophilia seen here. The classic picture is fever, rash, eosinophilia, sterile pyuria, and rising creatinine. NSAID-related cases often show fewer allergic signs than penicillin-related ones.
whyNot: Interferon-gamma comes from Th1 cells and activates macrophages, as in granulomas. It does not drive eosinophilia.
IL-17 from Th17 cells recruits neutrophils, which are not the dominant extra cell here.
IL-2 drives T-cell proliferation in general. It does not specifically produce eosinophils.
Correct.

questions.stem: A 24-hour urine collection contains 0.8 g of protein. Electrophoresis shows mostly beta2-microglobulin and other low-molecular-weight proteins, with little albumin. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: Impaired proximal reabsorption of small proteins
Lost size and charge selectivity of the glomerulus
Overproduction of monoclonal free light chains
approach: Small proteins like beta2-microglobulin pass the glomerulus freely and are normally taken back up by the proximal tubule.
Little albumin means the glomerular barrier is intact, which fits her normal glomeruli on biopsy.
Small proteins in the urine with intact glomeruli means the tubules are failing to reclaim them, which is tubular proteinuria.
questions.why: Proteinuria has three main patterns. Glomerular proteinuria is mostly albumin, because the damaged filter lets large proteins through. Overflow proteinuria happens when a small protein is made in such excess, as with light chains in myeloma, that it overwhelms tubular uptake. Tubular proteinuria happens when injured proximal tubules cannot endocytose the small proteins that are filtered every day, such as beta2-microglobulin, so they appear in urine. It is usually under 2 g/day and is poorly detected by dipstick, which mainly reads albumin.
whyNot: Correct.
Loss of glomerular size and charge selectivity lets albumin through and gives albumin-rich glomerular proteinuria. Her glomeruli are normal and albumin is low.
Monoclonal free light chains cause overflow proteinuria in multiple myeloma. Electrophoresis would show a single monoclonal band, not a mix of low-molecular-weight proteins.
Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin) is made by the thick ascending limb and is the normal matrix of casts. It is not beta2-microglobulin.

topics: Glomerular vs tubular vs overflow proteinuria

questions.stem: On the biopsy, tubulitis also involves a medullary segment lined by cuboidal cells with distinct lateral borders and no brush border. Most of its cells are pale with few organelles, and scattered cells are darker and rich in mitochondria. Which of the following segments is this?
approach: No brush border rules out the proximal tubule. Cuboidal cells rule out the thin limb, which is simple squamous.
Two different cell types in one lining is the key clue.
Pale principal cells mixed with dark, mitochondria-rich intercalated cells, with clear cell borders, mark the collecting duct.
questions.why: The collecting duct is lined by cuboidal to columnar cells with sharp lateral borders and no brush border. Most are principal cells, which stain pale and handle sodium and water under aldosterone and ADH. Scattered among them are intercalated cells, which stain darker because they are full of mitochondria that power H+ or HCO3- secretion. The proximal tubule has a brush border, the thin limb has a flat squamous lining, and the distal segments have a single cell type without a brush border.
whyNot: The proximal tubule has cuboidal cells with a tall brush border, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and many mitochondria, and its lateral borders are indistinct because the cells interdigitate.
Correct.
The thin descending limb is lined by simple squamous epithelium, so its cells are flat.
The thick ascending limb has one cell type, cuboidal and rich in mitochondria, without the mix of pale and dark cells.

questions.stem: Before the biopsy, which of the following urine sediment findings would most strongly have localized the source of her pyuria to the kidney?
options: Fatty casts with oval fat bodies
approach: Casts form only inside renal tubules, in a matrix of Tamm-Horsfall protein, so any cast places the process in the kidney.
The cells trapped in the cast tell you what the process is.
Leukocytes trapped in casts show that the white cells came from inflammation inside the kidney, as in interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis.
questions.why: Leukocytes in urine can come from anywhere along the tract, including the bladder and urethra. When they are trapped in a cast, they must have been in the tubule lumen, which places the inflammation in the kidney. White blood cell casts are seen in acute interstitial nephritis and pyelonephritis. Red blood cell casts point to glomerulonephritis, muddy brown granular casts to acute tubular necrosis, fatty casts to nephrotic syndrome, and waxy casts to chronic kidney disease.
whyNot: Red blood cell casts localize bleeding to the glomerulus and point to glomerulonephritis. They do not explain pyuria.
Muddy brown granular casts come from sloughed tubular cells in acute tubular necrosis. They do not show where white cells come from.
Correct.
Fatty casts and oval fat bodies come from lipiduria in nephrotic syndrome. She has only trace protein.
